Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an inherited condition characterized by the accumulation of fats called sulfatides in cells, especially cells of the nervous system. This accumulation results in progressive destruction of white matter of the brain, which consists of nerve fibers covered by myelin.Affected individuals experience progressive deterioration of intellectual functions and motor skills, such as the ability to walk. They also develop loss of sensation in the extremities, incontinence, seizures, paralysis, inability to speak, blindness, and hearing loss. Eventually they lose awareness of their surroundings and become unresponsive. This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and is caused by mutations in the ARSA and PSAP genes.

A genetic analysis revealed two mutations in the GM2A gene encoding the GM2 activator protein (GM2-AP), an essential co-factor of hexosaminidase A.

Two novel mutations in the GM2 activator gene (GM2A) have been identified by the reverse-transcriptase-PCR method--a three-base deletion, AAG262-264, resulting in a deletion of Lys88, and a single-base deletion, A410, that causes a frameshift.
Post-mortem genetic sequencing identified a pathogenic mutation in homozygosity in the GM2A gene, confirming the diagnosis.
Subsequent copy number analysis confirmed a homozygous deletion of exon 2 in GM2A.
Mutations in the human GM2 activator protein gene (GM2A) result in the GM2 gangliosidosis AB variant, a severe neurological disease.

The diagnosis of GM2 activator deficiency is established in a proband with suggestive findings of GM2 gangliosidosis, normal beta-hexosaminidase A (HEX A) enzyme activity levels, and biallelic pathogenic (or likely pathogenic) variants in GM2A identified by molecular genetic testing.

The GM2 activator is a hexosaminidase A-specific glycolipid-binding protein required for the lysosomal degradation of ganglioside GM2.
A deficiency of the GM2 activator causes the AB variant of GM2 gangliosidosis, a recessively inherited disorder characterized by excessive neuronal accumulation of GM2 and related glycolipids.
In contrast with these in vitro results the recombinant human GM2-activator is able to restore the degradation of GA2 in fibroblasts from patients with the AB variant of GM2 gangliosidosis in vivo.

GBA1 variants are among the most common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease (PD).
Among the lysosomal genes involved, GBA1 has the largest impact on Parkinson's disease risk.
different variants in the GBA1 gene can cause Parkinson's disease (PD, PARK-GBA1) with reduced penetrance, act as genetic risk factors for PD or parkinsonism, and/or lead to Gaucher's disease (GD).
Parkinson's disease patient derived neurons harboring mutant GBA1 exhibited prolonged mitochondria-lysosome contacts
GBA1 variants are common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease and also for dementia with Lewy bodies.
Mutations in GBA1 cause Gaucher disease and are the most important genetic risk factor for Parkinson's disease.
The exact mechanisms by which mutations in these genes cause PD are not fully understood.

Bi-allelic pathogenic GBA1 variants cause Gaucher disease (GD), whereas certain heterozygous missense variants increase the risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), although the underlying mechanisms are unclear.
Mutations in the GBA1 gene are common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease, disrupting enzymatic activity and causing lysosomal dysfunction, leading to elevated α-synuclein levels.
Gaucher disease (GD) is a rare hereditary lysosomal storage disease that arises due to deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.
Gaucher disease (GD) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease, caused by deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, required for the degradation of glycosphingolipids.

Globoid cell leukodystrophy or Krabbe is a disease that affects children as well as adults who have mutations in the gene encoding the enzyme galactosylceramidase/galctocerebrosidase (GALC), resulting in the deposition of the toxic lipid D-galactosyl-beta1-1' sphingosine (GalSph or psychosine).
The gene mutation occurs at chromosome 14, which codes for a lysosomal hydrolase known as galactosylceramide beta hydrolase (GALC).
It is caused by mutations on the galactocerebrosidase (GALC) gene.
Krabbe disease (KD) results from galactocerebrosidase (GALC) deficiency.
Krabbe disease is an autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by pathogenic variants in the galactocerebrosidase (GALC) gene.
Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy, GLD) is an inherited disease caused by a deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme galactocerebrosidase (GALC).
Functional experiments demonstrated that the variant led to impaired protein processing and localization, as well as reduced GALC enzymatic activity.
Tay-Sachs disease is a progressive, lethal neurodegenerative disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase-A that results in the accumulation of GM2 gangliosides.
Tay-Sachs disease (TSD) is an inherited neurological disorder caused by deficiency of hexosaminidase A (HexA).
Mechanistically, TSD is caused by mutations in the HEXA gene, which encodes the alpha subunit of hexosaminidase A.

A number of gene abnormalities responsible for Tay-Sachs disease have already been identified and the correlation between the beta-hexosaminidase alpha gene abnormality and the clinical phenotype has been explained in many cases.

Genetic testing subsequently revealed two heterozygous pathogenic mutations in the HEXA gene (c.1499delT p.(Leu500fs) and c.805G>A p.(Gly269Ser)), confirming the very rare diagnosis of adult-onset Tay-Sachs disease.
It results from mutations of the HEXA gene encoding the alpha subunit of beta-hexosaminidase, producing a destructive ganglioside accumulation in lysosomes, principally in neurons.

HEXA disorders are best considered as a disease continuum based on the amount of residual beta-hexosaminidase A (HEX A) enzyme activity. This, in turn, depends on the molecular characteristics and biological impact of the HEXA pathogenic variants.
This disease is caused by β-hexosaminidase A (HexA) enzyme deficiency due to various mutations in α-subunit gene of this enzyme
Tay-Sachs disease is a progressive, lethal neurodegenerative disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase-A that results in the accumulation of GM2 gangliosides.
This enables discovery of compounds that reduce GM2 and can lead to further development of a TSD therapy.
It is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A, which is responsible for the degradation of GM2 gangliosides-lipids that accumulate in the nerve cells of the central nervous system.
GM2-gangliosidosis is a group of neurological disorders resulting from genetically defective catabolism, and consequent abnormal accumulation, of GM2-ganglioside.
It results from mutations of the HEXA gene encoding the alpha subunit of beta-hexosaminidase, producing a destructive ganglioside accumulation in lysosomes, principally in neurons.
HEX A is necessary for degradation of GM2 ganglioside; without well-functioning enzymes, GM2 ganglioside builds up in the lysosomes of brain and nerve cells.
resulting in GM2 ganglioside accumulation predominantly in lysosomes of nerve cells

Fabry disease resulting from a deficiency of α-galactosidase A leads to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in various organs.
Fabry disease is induced by a mutation in the alpha-galactosidase A gene, causing a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A.

Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the α-galactosidase A (GLA) gene that leads to reduced or undetectable α-galactosidase A enzyme activity and progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide and its deacylated form
Fabry disease is an X-linked disorder in which lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A is lacking, leading to enzyme-substrate accumulation and tissues dysfunction.
Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that results from a deficiency of α-galactosidase A activity.
